## Results
The three key dimensions of the technological, organizational, and environmental framework were used to explore manufacturers’ perceptions of 3D apparel visualization software. The analysis revealed seven major categories, revealing how manufacturers perceive the value of the software for developing firefighting gear: relative advantage, technology maturity, and perceived future potential (Technological Context); organizational slack (Organizational Context); and industry characteristics, business partner readiness, and consumer perceptions (Environmental Context) (see Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#Tab2)). Due to the small, purposive sample (12 participants), the categories presented below are not generalizable to the broader population of firefighting gear manufacturers and should be viewed as context-specific and exploratory. The sections that follow present the categories associated with each context. Selected interview excerpts are included to support the findings, with participants identified by alphanumeric codes (e.g., A2, F1).
### Technological contexts: relative advantage, technology maturity, and perceived future potential
The technological context captures how participants evaluated the software’s immediate value and current limitations in relation to firefighting PPE design and decision-making. This section highlights how perceived benefits and concerns about capability shaped whether 3D apparel visualization software was viewed as a feasible support for development and communication.
#### Relative advantage
Relative advantage refers to the degree to which an innovation is perceived as being better than the idea or practice it replaces (Rogers, 1983). In this study, relative advantage was reflected in three sub-categories that captured participants’ positive expectations and beliefs about the performance of 3D apparel visualization software: (1) assistive tool for pattern optimization and sample development, (2) visualizing air gap distribution, and (3) enhancing sales interactions with municipalities.
##### Assistive tool for pattern optimization and sample development
Both experienced and inexperienced users highlighted usefulness of 3D apparel visualization software for adjusting grading rules, fitting patterns on multi-size avatars to streamline manual grading, aligning pattern segments, interpreting draglines, and refining multilayered composites for structural and wildland firefighting gear. Several participants also emphasized the potential of dynamic avatars to assess firefighters’ range of motion and to evaluate compliance with NFPA fit requirements. Some participants also noted that virtual fitting could significantly reduce the time and cost associated with producing physical samples, particularly for high-value structural gear. Participant C1 explained that their company invests heavily in structural gear samples, noting that “These garments cost between $3,000 and $4,000, so considerable effort goes into ensuring everything is correct before the fabric is cut.” Participant B2 highlighted that the software enabled more precise evaluation of multilayer pattern configurations during turnout coat development: “We could assess the positioning of the armscye, sleeves, and segment endpoints to verify alignment and determine whether modifying the relative positioning of layers would improve the design.” Participant D1 further indicated that the software had streamlined the process by eliminating fitting stages that previously required hours or days to complete.
##### Visualizing air gap distribution
In addition to improving internal efficiency, the software provided notable benefits for external communication. Although some participants identified the need to accurately visualize air gaps in turnout gear as a challenge to adoption, others emphasized the value of 3D apparel visualization software in illustrating the volume and distribution of air gaps between the wearer and the structural ensemble, particularly through cross-sectional views and transparent material settings. Participant E1 noted that determining an optimal air gap that balances thermal protection and mobility remains an ongoing topic of discussion within the NFPA committee. Participant A1 stated that 3D apparel visualization software has the potential to facilitate consensus in this field as visual aids in technical discussions: “Some committee members assume that reducing a garment detail will make the entire uniform fit tightly. 3D virtual simulation image clarifies this misunderstanding by visualizing garment-to-body space and showing how to balance mobility with functional air gaps.”
##### Enhancing sales interactions with municipalities
Some participants proposed using images generated through 3D apparel visualization software to support discussions of product features when engaging with decision-makers from municipalities, fire departments, and county agencies. Participant B1 noted that virtual prototyping allows sales teams to present visual representations to customers without incurring the costs associated with fabric and labor. She explained:
> There is no clear visual representation of the gear until the department finalizes its purchase decision and specifications. With virtual prototyping, once those specifications are established, we can generate and present a 3D rendering of the product to show what the gear will look like.
#### Technology maturity
Despite the perceived advantages, participants reported that adoption is hindered by a lack of technology maturity. Technology maturity refers to the degree to which a technological architecture is sufficiently developed and ready for deployment within a firm (Schmitt et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR85 "Schmitt, G., Mladenow, A., Strauss, C., & Schaff hauser-Linzatti, M. \(2019\). Smart contracts and internet of things: A qualitative content analysis using the technology-organization-environment framework to identify key-determinants. Procedia Computer Science, 160, 189–196. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procs.2019.09.460
                  
                "), p. 193). In the present study, technology maturity was reflected in a sub-category that captured participants’ concerns about 3D apparel visualization software: simulation fidelity for composite materials, multilayer garments, and air gaps.
##### Simulation fidelity for composite materials, multilayer garments, and air gaps
A central concern among companies producing structural turnout gear was the limited capacity of current software to accurately simulate three-layer composite systems, seam construction, and the substantial ease and air gaps required for thermal protection. Structural turnout gear is composed of an outer shell, moisture barrier, and thermal liner, each contributing to overall performance (McQuerry et al., [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR41 "McQuerry, M., DenHartog, E., & Barker, R. \(2017\). Evaluating turnout composite layering strategies for reducing thermal burden in structural firefighter protective clothing systems. Textile Research Journal, 87\(10\), 1217–1225. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0040517516651101
                  
                ")). Participant C2 explained that the thickness of these layered materials influences seam construction, allowances, and sewing techniques, thereby increasing production complexity. Participant B2, who attempted to model the three layers by individually constructing and stacking pattern components, described the process as cumbersome: “We can assemble the patterns into a single product, but we can’t realistically observe how they hang on the body [in a simulation] because of the layering.”
The accurate representation of air gaps was also identified as a major challenge, as these spaces are critical for thermal protection. Participant C1 noted, “The wearer’s chest circumference is 44 inches, but the coat should measure 52 inches to maintain an adequate air buffer.” Participants emphasized that the degree of looseness required by safety standards makes it difficult to evaluate fit using 3D apparel visualization software. They also questioned the relevance of garment-fit maps, such as stress and strain indicators, which are more suited to body-conforming apparel than to protective garments designed with intentional and substantial ease.
In addition, participants pointed to the need for improved functionality to simulate the multiple garment layers worn in conjunction with turnout gear. Participant D1 expressed a desire for future systems to support stable multi-layer modeling of components such as fire hoods, suspenders, aluminized gear, and self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA). Collectively, these concerns highlight a gap between the current capabilities of 3D apparel visualization software and the specialized requirements of firefighting gear design.
#### Perceived future potential
Perceived future potential refers not to the current benefits that 3D apparel visualization software can provide, but to the hoped-for, future-oriented value that may emerge as the software evolves or is integrated with other systems and applications. This construct captures participants’ expectations for expanded capabilities or new functions they would like to see developed. In the present study, perceived future potential was reflected in two sub-categories: (1) predicting thermal protection and water penetration performance, and (2) enabling customization and enhancing customer engagement.
##### Predicting thermal protection and water penetration performance
Participants emphasized the need for the technology to transition from a primarily visual design tool to a performance-oriented evaluation platform. Participant C1 highlighted the potential of integrating predictive capabilities for thermal performance metrics, such as breathability and total heat loss. Participant C2 underscored this need, noting: “We allocate substantial resources to third-party testing for NFPA certification. It would be highly advantageous if the software could model how pattern modifications influence thermal and water penetration performance within a 3D simulation environment.”
Participant F1 further indicated that predictive modeling could enhance design decision-making, explaining that the ability to anticipate water penetration patterns during shower tests would support more effective pattern adjustments. He emphasized the potential to use such metrics to inform ventilation design and more sophisticated pattern engineering, while accounting for the interaction between garment construction and real-world fireground conditions.
##### Enabling customization and enhancing customer engagement
Participants further anticipated that future advancements could facilitate mass customization by enabling client-facing interfaces through which fire departments can directly specify gear configurations, reducing miscommunication and enhancing customer interaction. Two companies (E and F) were already providing customized firefighting gear. Participant E1 noted that current ordering processes rely on written or verbal exchanges with sales representatives, which can lead to misinterpretation. They expressed interest in developing “a 3D platform that allows customers to customize various elements of their gear and submit their designs for quotation.”
### Organizational contexts: organizational slack
Moving beyond perceptions of the technology itself, participants emphasized that adoption also depends on organizational conditions, particularly whether firms have sufficient discretionary resources to invest in licenses, infrastructure, and workforce upskilling. In this context, feasibility was discussed in terms of capacity to implement and sustain the workflow change.
#### Organizational slack
Participants reported that adoption decisions are heavily influenced by organizational slack. Organizational slack refers to the pool of uncommitted resources that a firm can draw upon to support new initiatives or innovations (Oliveira & Martins, [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR51 "Oliveira, T., & Martins, M. F. \(2011\). Literature review of information technology adoption models at firm level. Electronic Journal of Information Systems Evaluation, 14\(1\), 110–121.")). In this study, organizational slack was reflected in two sub-categories: (1) financial costs, and (2) human capital investment.
##### Financial costs
Participants unanimously identified cost as the predominant barrier, with smaller firms struggling to justify the high price of software licenses and peripheral hardware (e.g., fabric testing devices, texture scanners) against the perceived return on investment, irrespective of their current usage status. Participant D1 articulated concerns, noting, “Our current system functions effectively, making it challenging to justify the annual software license fee, which previously quoted at $13,000.” For small- or medium-scale manufacturers operating within budget constraints, funds were prioritized for essential manufacturing production operations rather than for experimental 3D apparel visualization software over design or product innovation.
On the other hand, participants suggested that companies belonging to larger-scale firms would be willing to bear the cost if it was proven that using the software could improve the product quality. Participant F1 mentioned, “I believe that the software license fee is easily affordable for our company, and they are willing to invest heavily in proving that our product is the safest option available.” However, at the same time, he expected it would be challenging to communicate and prove the effectiveness of the software to the company decision-makers.
##### Human capital investment
Beyond financial costs, participants reported that the human capital investment required for implementation presented a significant hurdle. Both current users and non-users highlighted the steep learning curve and the substantial time required to upskill employees. Integrating the software into existing workflows demanded not just financial readiness but also a willingness to divert limited staff hours away from immediate production tasks to master complex new systems.
### Environmental contexts: industry characteristics, business partner readiness, and consumer perception
Finally, participants emphasized that adoption is influenced not only by internal readiness but also by environmental conditions, such as industry norms, partner capabilities, and end-user requirements. This section shows how ecosystem readiness and stakeholder acceptance can enable or constrain adoption even when the technology is promising and internal resources are available.
#### Industry characteristics
Within the TOE framework, industry characteristics refer to the structural and competitive attributes of the focal industry such as market structure, competitive intensity, regulatory policies, stakeholder pressures, industry life-cycle stage, and the availability of technology-related support that shape the external pressures and opportunities influencing innovation adoption (Gupta et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR79 "Gupta, S., Ghardallou, W., Pandey, D. K., & Sahu, G. P. \(2022\). Artifi cial intelligence adoption in the insurance industry: Evidence using the technology–organization–environment framework. ##### Unchanging garment style requirements
Unlike the fashion industry, where rapid style turnover drives the need for quick digital sampling, firefighting gear designs remain static for decades. Participant A2 noted, “Once we achieve a well-fitted shirt and pants, there's little need for alteration.” Similarly, Participant F1 observed, “Our repeat customers typically return every 5 or 10 years, requesting identical products.” and Participant C1 stated, “Our patterns have been 30 years old. Although we have newer patterns for new products, they possess similar properties.” Consequently, the infrequent need to adjust patterns or experiment with diverse virtual fabrics limits the utility of virtual fitting for pattern modifications or exploring fabric drapability and fit. The enduring nature of unaltered garment styles restricts the potential benefits and frequency of leveraging virtual fitting capabilities, as highlighted by participants.
##### Normative conservatism
Several participants perceived the firefighting gear industry as placing limited emphasis on design innovation and research. They noted that decision-makers tend to be conservative and less open to new technologies, partly due to the sector’s strong safety orientation. Participant E2 observed, “The scarcity of specialized designers for firefighter gear underscores its niche status.” Participant F1 mentioned, “A challenge in implementing this type of technology in this industry is overcoming the conservative mindset. Since safety is paramount, they tend to have a conservative mindset and are less receptive to new technology.” Participant E1 observed that the computer-aided design software used in the firefighting gear manufacturing industry lags compared to fields such as aerospace, automotive, and construction, reinforcing challenges to advancing innovative practices.

##### Preparedness among contract manufacturers
Some participants expressed concern that manufacturers may lack the readiness to access and interpret data generated by 3D apparel visualization software. Participants A1 and A2 noted that their company’s reliance on contract manufacturers could limit their ability to adopt such technology. Participant A2 explained that the software is still unfamiliar within the firefighting gear industry, which may lead to implementation challenges and potential issues. They stated:

#### Consumer perception
Consumer perception refers to end users’ attitudes toward innovative technologies (Schmitt et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR85 "Schmitt, G., Mladenow, A., Strauss, C., & Schaff hauser-Linzatti, M. \(2019\). ##### Skepticism toward virtual simulation in customer-facing marketing
None of the participants viewed virtual simulation images as effective for marketing on websites, social media, or product catalogs. They expressed that the industry culture heavily favors “real-world” testimonials and physical handling of gear over digital simulations, limiting the technology’s effectiveness as a marketing tool unless it can be proven to accurately reflect physical performance. Participant A2 explained that using simulated or artificial models would not effectively support building a genuine connection with the firefighter community. Similarly, Participant E4 noted that their company deliberately features real firefighters, emphasizing that their lived experience with the gear enhances credibility among other firefighters.
Several categories and subcategories within the TOE framework were identified as shaping firefighting gear manufacturers’ perceptions of 3D apparel visualization software. Within the technological context, participants viewed 3D apparel visualization software as a performance-oriented tool suited to the unique demands of protective gear. They highlighted its potential to optimize patterns for bulky, multilayered ensembles, visualize air gap distribution, and use dynamic avatars to assess mobility and NFPA fit compliance. Participants also noted value in using 3D apparel visualization software as a sales aid when meeting with municipal buyers and fire departments. Looking ahead, they anticipated future capabilities such as predicting thermal and water-penetration performance and enabling more interactive customization.
In terms of the organizational context, adoption was limited by financial constraints, the need to upskill staff, and the challenge of integrating 3D apparel visualization software into existing workflows that would support digital assets and simulation processes. For the environmental context, the industry’s niche, safety-driven culture, stable garment designs, and reliance on contract manufacturers unfamiliar with 3D virtual simulation data reduced perceived necessity and feasibility. Participants also noted that firefighters and municipal buyers prefer marketing featuring real firefighters, making simulated imagery less persuasive. ## Discussion
Overall, this study provides insight into how firefighting PPE manufacturers evaluate the adoption of 3D apparel visualization software and the conditions that shape its feasibility in a safety–critical, standards-constrained product domain. Consistent with TOE-based technology adoption research, participants’ evaluations reflected an interaction among technological characteristics, organizational readiness, and environmental constraints. However, rather than viewing 3D apparel visualization software as a direct substitute for physical sampling and testing, participants framed it as a complementary capability whose perceived relative advantage and compatibility depend on two domain-specific requirements: effective integration with established verification routines (e.g., wear trials, iterative sampling, and performance compliance testing) and acceptance by key external stakeholders as a credible visual aid for supporting regulatory communication, sales interactions, and customer engagement. Taken together, these findings suggest that in regulated, high-risk manufacturing contexts, TOE constructs such as relative advantage and compatibility are shaped by legitimacy and validation expectations that extend beyond the firm to the broader industry community and supply chain.
Consistent with classic TOE theorizing, manufacturers emphasized relative advantage as a necessary but insufficient condition for adoption (Rogers, 1983; Tornatzky & Fleischer, 1990). Participants recognized clear performance benefits of 3D apparel visualization software, including pattern optimization, air gap visualization, and improved communication with municipal buyers. Within the organizational context, the findings underscore organizational slack as a pivotal factor shaping adoption. Company size further impacted how the TOE dimensions interacted. In TOE terms, this suggests that organizational readiness cannot be fully understood without considering the environmental conditions that shape managerial perceptions of the strategic necessity of innovation.
Company type (firefighting gear type) further influenced these evaluations through the organizational dimension. For wildland gear manufacturers (Companies A and D), whose products involve relatively simple, single-layer constructions, the technology presented low perceived complexity and minimal strategic relevance. Structural turnout gear manufacturers (Companies B, C, E, and F), however, confronted high technological complexity due to multilayer composites and intricate construction requirements. This complexity simultaneously intensified skepticism about current simulation fidelity and elevated expectations for future capabilities such as garment fit maps and performance prediction including inter-garment tension, total heat loss, water penetration, and wearer fit satisfaction during pattern design. Structural turnout gear production heightened both perceived technological barriers and perceived technological advantage, reflecting the ambivalent role of innovation complexity in shaping adoption intentions.
The study findings also underscore the importance of the environmental context in ways that extend typical TOE applications. Firefighting gear manufacturers operate within stringent standards, liability concerns, and procurement norms, all which frame how new technologies are interpreted and assessed. These environmental pressures intersected with product characteristics to shape firms’ evaluations of technological attributes. Manufacturers of wildland gear viewed 3D apparel visualization software as offering mainly incremental improvements in pattern making. In contrast, structural turnout gear manufacturers faced far higher technical demands due to multilayer composites and strict thermal performance requirements. For them, 3D apparel visualization software elicited both heightened expectations and deeper skepticism: it was imagined as a promising tool for fit mapping and performance prediction, yet current software was widely regarded as technically inadequate. This ambivalence suggests that greater product complexity can simultaneously amplify perceived relative advantage and perceived complexity, creating an innovation tension within the technological domain.

Technological limitations such as imperfect simulation of composite materials, air gap layers, and multilayer garments shaped organizational risk assessments, which were then evaluated within environmental regimes that demand strong evidence of safety and compliance. Even when 3D apparel visualization software is viewed as beneficial for design efficiency, manufacturers remain cautious if the tools do not clearly support, or are not formally recognized within, established performance evaluation and certification processes. These intersecting factors reinforce the importance of considering structural heterogeneity when applying the TOE framework to understand how firefighting gear manufacturers assess the feasibility and strategic value of 3D apparel visualization software.

This study also complements research on 3D apparel visualization software, which has largely emphasized technical capabilities and design benefits (Hakeem et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR19 "Hakeem, F., Xia, S., & Stannard, C. \(2024\). Evaluating 3D apparel simulation technology’s performance of creative pattern-cutting techniques with the assistance of ASVT. Advance online publication. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0887302X241278929
                  
                "); Lee & Park, [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR32 "Lee, S. H., & Park, J. \(2025\). Ergonomic block patterns for older women’s athleisure pants: Applying the 3D surface flattening and pattern reduction method. Advance online publication. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0887302X251351356
                  
                "); Viziteu & Curteza, [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00469-8#ref-CR69 "Viziteu, D. R., & Curteza, A. \(2021\). Development of climbing clothes using computerized 3D clothing simulation. Art and Design, 2, 9–19. 
                  https://doi.org/10.30857/2617-0272.2021.2.1
                  
                ")), while giving comparatively less attention to organizational and industry-level adoption dynamics. The findings demonstrate that, in functional and safety–critical apparel contexts, adoption is shaped by the interaction of multiple TOE-based mechanisms. These include technological factors such as simulation fidelity for multilayer systems and air gap representation; organizational factors such as internal expertise, resource availability, and workflow integration; and environmental factors such as regulatory expectations, partner readiness, and user trust. Within this configuration, the perceived credibility and legitimacy of digital outputs play a central role. As a result, technical capability alone is insufficient to explain adoption. The same 3D tool may be interpreted as a low-risk communication aid or as a high-stakes performance-evidence system depending on product complexity, organizational capacity, and perceived regulatory scrutiny.
More broadly, the study highlights the relevance of these mechanisms beyond the immediate context of firefighting gear. In functional and protective apparel sectors where product performance is closely tied to regulation, specialized materials, and interorganizational coordination, adoption is likely to be shaped by similar interactions among technological readiness, organizational capacity, and environmental legitimacy. In this sense, the contribution of the study lies not in statistical generalizability but in the transferability of these TOE-based mechanisms to other safety–critical apparel domains, such as military, industrial, or medical protective clothing. At the same time, these implications should be interpreted within the scope of the present study. The findings are based on qualitative interviews with a small sample of U.S. firefighting gear manufacturers and therefore reflect a context-specific analysis. The insights are most applicable to sectors that share comparable technological constraints, regulatory environments, and supply-chain structures, rather than to the apparel industry as a whole.
The findings also highlight practical implications for software developers, manufacturers, and regulatory bodies. For developers, closer collaboration with protective clothing manufacturers and textile laboratories is needed to improve the physics-based modeling of multilayer composites and to strengthen validation by linking simulations to established metrics such as Thermal Protective Performance (TPP) and Total Heat Loss (THL). These improvements could support the transition of 3D apparel visualization software from a communication-focused tool to a platform capable of informing performance-oriented design decisions. In addition, vendors may reduce adoption barriers by offering modular features, streamlined onboarding processes, and technical support that extends to contract manufacturers and other supply-chain partners.
For regulatory bodies such as NFPA and related standards committees, the findings underscore the importance of considering how virtual prototyping tools may complement, rather than replace, existing certification processes. Providing clear guidance on the appropriate use of 3D apparel visualization software in early-stage design, for example as a screening tool prior to physical TPP and THL testing, could reduce perceived risk and encourage adoption. Over time, the development of standardized practices for documenting digital simulations, input parameters, and validation procedures may enable more systematic integration of virtual evidence into design and certification workflows.
Despite these contributions, several limitations should be acknowledged. The study focuses on firm-level perspectives and relies on a single data source, interviews with a relatively small sample, which constrains the scope of the findings. The limited diversity of the sample suggests that the results should be interpreted as exploratory and context-specific rather than representative of the broader industry. In addition, the concentration of participant roles, primarily designers and technical specialists, limits insight into perspectives from production, marketing, and executive decision-making. Some participants also had limited direct experience with 3D apparel visualization software, which may have influenced their perceptions.
Future research should continue to evaluate the validity and accuracy of virtual simulation technologies while expanding beyond a single national context. Advancing 3D apparel visualization software for firefighting gear will require improvements in simulation precision, enhanced garment fit mapping, and more standardized methods for digitizing multilayer composite materials and trims. Identifying the optimal air gap that balances thermal protection and mobility remains a critical step for informing fit standards and improving simulation accuracy. At the same time, fit map functionality should be further developed to better predict garment tension and stress distribution while incorporating air gap parameters.
To strengthen the robustness and broader applicability of this research, future studies could adopt mixed-methods designs that integrate qualitative insights with quantitative and experimental approaches. Comparing virtual simulation outputs with laboratory-based measurements of thermal performance, air gap distribution, and mobility would provide important validation benchmarks. Larger-scale surveys and comparative studies across different regions, including Europe and Asia, would further clarify how regulatory environments and industry structures shape technology adoption. These efforts would contribute to the development of more reliable simulation tools and more widely applicable guidelines for virtual prototyping in protective clothing design.

# Analysis of Woven Fabric Mechanical Properties in the Context of Sustainable Clothing Development Process

## Abstract

This paper presents research in the field of computer-aided 3D clothing design, focusing on an investigation of three methods for determining the mechanical properties of woven fabrics and their impact on 3D clothing simulations in the context of sustainable apparel development. Five mechanical parameters were analyzed: tensile elongation in the warp and weft directions, shear stiffness, bending stiffness, specific weight, and fabric thickness. These parameters were integrated into the CLO3D CAD software v.2025.0.408, using data obtained via the KES-FB system, the Fabric Kit protocol, and the AI-based tool, SEDDI Textura 2024. Simulations of women’s blouse and trousers were evaluated using dynamic tests and validated by real prototypes measured with the ARAMIS optical 3D system. Results show average differences between digital and real prototype deformation data up to 6% with an 8% standard deviation, confirming the high accuracy of 3D simulations based on the determined mechanical parameters of the real fabric sample. Notably, the AI-based method demonstrated excellent simulation results compared with real garments, highlighting its potential for accessible, sustainable, and scalable fabric digitization. Presented research is entirely in line with the current trends of digitization and sustainability in the textile industry. It contributes to the advancement of efficient digital prototyping workflows and emphasizes the importance of reliable mechanical characterization for predictive garment modeling.

Keywords: woven fabric, mechanical properties, AI technology, 3D simulations, digital prototyping, dynamic deformations

## 1. Introduction

The advancement of computer technologies and CAD systems for 2D/3D garment design has significantly transformed the field of clothing engineering. These innovations have enabled the development of digital 3D prototypes and fit analysis, facilitating the prediction of both the appearance and functionality of garments prior to physical production. The adoption of digital methodologies in garment development significantly contributes to the sustainability of the manufacturing process, addressing the traditional challenges of material waste, time consumption, and financial costs associated with the iterative creation of physical prototypes. Traditionally, garment design and development involve a cyclical process requiring multiple iterations of pattern adjustments and the physical testing of numerous prototypes to achieve the desired garment form and fit. This traditional approach can become especially resource-intensive when dealing with complex designs, as it relies on extensive material usage and manual labor.

In contrast, one of the most notable advantages of CAD systems is their capability to simulate and evaluate the fit of garments directly on 3D virtual human models, without the need for physical samples. Furthermore, these systems allow the assessment of fabric properties in relation to the targeted textile material, thereby facilitating the selection of fabrics based on their physical and mechanical characteristics [,]. According to different research and case studies, the implementation of digital prototyping in apparel product development reduces the time of pattern making by 85% and the number of physical samples up to a 60–80% (on average from 3–5 to 1–2 samples), thus significantly reducing material waste, energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions in the development phase. Saving on sample transport between designers and manufacturers further reduces greenhouse gas emissions and energy costs [,,,]. The integration of digital prototyping with Industry 4.0 technologies enables resource optimization, sustainability monitoring, and CO2 emission reduction through transparent and shortened supply chains, confirming that digital prototyping contributes not only to waste reduction but also to achieving circular economy goals [,].

Leading CAD systems, such as Lectra, Optitex, Assyst, CLO3D, and Browzwear, offer comprehensive digital solutions that support the entire garment development process, from 2D pattern construction and 3D body simulation to virtual fitting and integration with marketing channels. These systems are also increasingly employed for virtual fashion shows and online retail visualizations, enabling early-stage product validation and consumer engagement [,,,,]. Garment simulation involves physical simulation of joining 2D pattern pieces around a 3D body model, based on algorithms that give virtual garments realistic physical behavior, taking into account forces such as gravity, collisions, and mass []. Common simulation techniques are based on elasticity theory, particle-spring systems, and finite element methods (FEM), which are particularly well suited to modeling complex draping and fabric deformation [,,]. The research by Volino and Magnenat Thalmann is particularly significant in developing textile and clothing simulation methods based on elasticity theory and Newtonian dynamics [,,]. Finite element methods are also frequently used to model complex textile deformations and draping [,,].

Given the inherently anisotropic and deformable nature of textiles, simulating the behavior of clothing remains a very complex physical problem. Textiles exhibit significant variations in their technical characteristics, including fiber content, weave structure, yarn density, thickness, and weight, which affect both their manufacturing and wear properties. Mechanical properties are crucial for selecting appropriate materials based on garment design and function. Accurate simulation necessitates the quantification of fabric mechanical properties under low-stress conditions, which are typical during garment handling and wearing [,,]. The main mechanical properties affecting textile behaviour are tensile, bending, shear, and compression properties, along with specific weight and thickness as physical parameters. These characteristics determine the fabric’s response to external forces and are thus essential for accurate virtual prototyping. Since textiles in processing and use are subject to low loads, linearity parameters are key metrics in evaluating processing and performance properties. Thus, tensile values in the linear region along warp and weft directions are most commonly applied for 3D garment simulations. Fabric bending properties depend on composition, construction, and finishing methods, such as dyeing, printing, or surface coatings. Bending stiffness (B), which defines resistance to bending under its weight, is a commonly used parameter for 3D simulations. Shear properties are essential for achieving a proper 3D garment shape, draping, pliability and hand. Shear deformation results from inter-yarn angle changes, and shear stress in the linear range is expressed using shear stiffness. Compression properties in 3D simulation are defined by fabric thickness, measured as the distance between two parallel planes under two different given loads [,,,].

From the perspective of computer graphics, textile materials in a CAD system for 3D simulation are described as a mesh of polygons with a specified density (i.e., the size of a particular polygon), where each polygon represents a solid surface corresponding to the fabric’s mass. The polygons are interconnected, and the joints between them behave according to the predefined parameters of the fabric’s physical and mechanical properties [,]. The quality of a 3D simulation and the ability to predict garment appearance and behaviour heavily depend on the algorithm and number of material parameters each CAD system uses, as well as the method for testing those parameters [,]. Tools like the Kawabata Evaluation System (KES-FB), the FAST system, and, more recently, user-friendly devices such as the Fabric Kit and Fabric Testing Utilities integrated into specific CAD software platforms are commonly employed for capturing mechanical parameters in clothing simulations [,,]. Recent research has explored the integration of machine learning algorithms for predicting fabric properties from minimal input parameters, enhancing simulation efficiency. By leveraging extensive datasets, these intelligent systems can correlate physical and mechanical attributes, reducing reliance on complex physical testing [,,].

Numerous comparative studies have assessed the fidelity of various systems and parameter sets in replicating real fabric behavior through 3D simulations [,,,,,,]. Surface mesh density parameters significantly influence the simulation quality and realistic behavior [,,]. To evaluate 3D simulation results, many studies use complex draping deformation analyses. Kenkara et al. reported that drape parameters vary for each test and that a variability of up to 15% when comparing simulation and real values is acceptable accuracy. Their study was conducted on 20 different fabrics using the Cusick Drape Meter and 3D scanning technology []. Thi et al. evaluated drape parameters for six fabrics using V Stitcher []. Buyukaslan et al. analyzed drape simulations for five fabrics using the FAST method and the Optitex CAD system. Based on the subjective assessment of the draping parameters and the overall appearance of the simulated samples in comparison with real samples, a satisfactory level of accuracy of the performed 3D simulations was determined, according to Kenkare’s similarity criterion of 15% [,]. Rudolf et al. studied the impact of simulation algorithm settings on the simulated skirt model behavior in the Optitex CAD system, based on a comparison between digital and real prototypes, using orthogonal projection areas and length measurements at different positions as metric parameters [].

To evaluate the computer prototypes and 3D simulation results, various comparisons and evaluation criteria of similarity between the digital and real prototypes are most often used in research [,]. Various CAD systems for 3D garment design offer fit analysis tools such as cross-sectioning of a digital garment prototype on a body model, where the amount and distribution of garment ease allowance can be determined from the differences in the circumference values. Analysis of the garment pressure against the body and surface deformations, such as warp or weft elongations, enables fit assessment in relation to the parameters of the mechanical properties of the woven material being simulated [,]. Zangue et al. investigated the possibilities of digital prototypes fit analysis, using the example of a men’s jacket and comparison of the results obtained using three different CAD systems for garment design []. In their paper, they point out that the assessment of the digital prototypes’ fit is a major challenge that requires a combination of understanding of simulation algorithms and knowledge and experience in garment design and construction. Kim et al. developed an evaluation method based on the comparison of digital and real prototypes of a skirt model using 3D scanning technology for better measurement accuracy. A special contribution of the method is the set of subjective evaluation criteria for the prototype’s appearance and its correlation with objective mechanical parameter values, resulting in a regression equation for evaluating 3D prototypes []. Lapkovska and Dabolina also conducted an evaluation study of 3D simulations by comparing computer and simulated prototypes of skirt models, using the parameters of the shape and dimensions of the model cross-sections at different heights as a comparative criterion. They also applied 3D scanning technology to analyze the real prototypes because it is not possible to simply and precisely determine the shape and dimensions of the garment cross-sections using the conventional methods due to the folds of the material [].

Despite notable advancements in virtual analysis of garment fit, limitations remain, particularly in the objective assessment of digital prototypes during motion. However, validation techniques such as 3D scanning and optical measurement systems, such as those used in the presented study, offer promising approaches to quantitatively evaluating virtual fit. The number of studies dealing with the objective assessment of the dynamic fit of computer prototypes and their evaluation in terms of comparing the deformations of simulated and real prototypes of clothing models is very limited, given that testing real garments in this sense is very complex and there are no dedicated methods for analysing the deformations of a garment on a moving body in wearing conditions. Pioneering approaches involving 4D scanning and motion capture have introduced methods for overlaying dynamic garment geometries on moving body models [,,]. Klepster et al. developed a clothing fit assessment method during movement, using 4D body scanning. They recorded participants performing movements wearing underwear and conventional upper garments; scans in underwear defined a baseline body shape, and scans in clothing captured possible body restrictions. Using Geomagic Studio 2012 software, overlaying dressed and undressed 4D scans enabled analysis of air gaps and surface penetration, indicating potential restrictions. However, this method is complex, time-consuming, and results depend heavily on participant movement reproducibility, limiting its application to simple movements []. Zhang et al. proposed a numerical evaluation method for digital garment prototypes based on surface geometry alignment with 4D-scanned models. They created a simplified kinematic skeleton for animating body surface models, facilitating the overlay of dressed and undressed models. Body motion was defined using point translations and rotations over time, from 4D scans. The undressed model was used to simulate trousers in three movements, which were then overlapped with scans of real trousers during the same movements. Fit was analyzed based on stretch and deformation criteria and overall garment appearance []. Terrier developed a FEM-based simulation method for a cycling bodysuit using Abaqus and verified its accuracy using the ARAMIS optical system, which captures 3D deformations commonly used in mechanical and civil engineering and construction. The focus was on analysing compression zones where elastic tapes support the body during cycling [,]. Presented methods, though promising, face challenges related to data processing complexity, motion repeatability, and the precise alignment of body and garment geometries. Overall, while current CAD-based garment simulation tools offer significant potential for sustainable, cost-effective, and accurate garment development, the field continues to evolve. Future research should focus on improving dynamic fit modelling, standardizing mechanical property measurement methods, and advancing intelligent systems for fabric property prediction.

In this study, the potential for integrating and defining fabric mechanical parameters within the 3D garment simulation and design environment, CLO3D, was explored to evaluate the influence of different measurement approaches on the results and accuracy of digital clothing prototypes. Mechanical property values for a selected woven fabric sample were determined using three distinct evaluation methods: The Kawabata Evaluation System (KES-FB), the Fabric Kit method, and the artificial intelligence-based application SEDDI Textura 2024. The obtained values were used to define the mechanical behaviour of the fabric during 3D clothing simulation in the CLO3D environment. To validate the resulting digital simulations, the ARAMIS optical 3D measurement system was employed to analyse the dynamic deformation of physical garment prototypes, i.e., base models of a woman’s blouse and trousers. The analysis focused on assessing the degree of accuracy and correlation between simulated and real prototypes’ deformations under dynamic conditions, depending on the method used to derive the fabric parameters. The hypothesis underpinning this work is that fabric properties obtained via AI-assisted evaluation will result in the most realistic simulation outcomes, producing digital prototype deformations that most accurately reflect those observed in physical prototypes subjected to movement. The findings of this study contribute to ongoing efforts to improve the fidelity of 3D garment simulations and to establish best practices for parameterization based on available measurement technologies.

## 2. Materials and Methods

### 2.1. Analysis of Textile Material Properties for 3D Simulation

A twill-woven fabric composed of blended fibres, intended for women’s outerwear, was selected for testing. All fabric test samples were pre-conditioned and tested under the standard testing conditions of 20 ± 2 °C temperature and 65 ± 4% relative humidity. The percentage of components is given in . The fibre composition was qualitatively confirmed through microscopy analysis using specific reagents, employing an Olympus BX51 universal microscope with a DP50 digital camera and image analysis software, AnalySIS 2002. The warp yarn consists of pure cotton, while the weft yarn consists of elastane filaments wrapped with polyester fibres, as shown in a,b.

#### 2.1.2. Investigation of Fabric Tensile and Shear Properties Using a Fabric Kit Adapted Method

The fabric was further evaluated using the parameters defined by the Fabric Kit measurement system, designed for CLO3D. Although original Fabric Kit devices were not used, tensile and shear parameters were determined using a tensile testing machine, Tensolab 3000, Mesdan S.p.A. (Raffa, Italy), with testing conditions aligned to Fabric Kit guidelines: a 120 mm grip separation and specimen dimensions of 270 × 30 mm, tested in warp, weft, and bias directions. Force readings were performed during five consecutive extensions of 1 or 10 mm, depending on the elasticity of the fabric. The method prescribes that if a force of less than 0.098 N is required to stretch the material by 1 mm (elongation of 0.83%), the force is recorded at five consecutive elongations of 10 mm each (8.33%), or at each increase in force of 0.196 N. If a force greater than 0.098 N is required to stretch the material by 1 mm, the force is recorded at five consecutive elongations of 1 mm each (0.83%) [,]. The determined results of five consecutive readings of the force values required for defined increments of elongation of the test specimen were entered into the Emulator module within the CLO3D software, which converts the entered values into supported units of measurement and creates a compatible data format of the new digital material for application in 3D clothing simulation processes, as shown in .

#### 2.1.3. Digitization of Textile Material Using the SEDDI Textura AI Application

The SEDDI Textura AI application was used to digitize the selected woven fabric based on scanned surface images and input of basic data: fibre composition, weave type, areal weight, and thickness [,]. The method integrates photogrammetry, spectrometry, and computer vision to extract detailed surface geometry and optical reflectance data from scanned images of textile materials. These data, in combination with manually input data on fiber composition and basic physical parameters, are processed through a deep learning algorithm that trains a neural network to generate parameters suitable for physically based rendering. A key advantage of the AI method lies in its use of a multimodal dataset that combines visual, spectrometric, and mechanical properties of textiles, thereby capturing a broad spectrum of real-world material variations. The neural network is trained on a large number of samples with diverse textures, thicknesses, fiber compositions, and mechanical characteristics. This enables the model to generalize fabric behavior beyond the original dataset. The final result is a digital texture ready for direct integration into 3D CAD software, containing data for realistic visual representation and assessed values of material mechanical parameters for 3D garment simulation [,]. Digital prototypes simulated using mechanical parameters determined by the KES-FB system showed higher deformation values compared to the results of the real prototypes analysis. In contrast, simulations using parameters obtained using the Fabric Kit methodology showed lower deformations compared to the real prototypes, as shown in , , and . When comparing the KES-FB and Fabric Kit methodologies, the main difference lies in the value of the maximum force applied during the analysis. In the testing of tensile and shear properties, the maximum force applied by the KES system is 490.35 N/m. However, in the Fabric Kit method, by tracking five consecutive elongations of 1 or 10 mm (depending on the test sample), higher forces are recorded compared to the maximum force used in the KES-FB system. Due to the limited maximum force, it is not possible to extract force values for five consecutive elongations of 1 or 10 mm from the F/ε diagram, and parameters obtained from the KES-FB system cannot be imported into the CLO3D software using the Emulator.

When observing the converted parameter values imported in CLO3D, as shown in and , it is evident that the stress values derived from the KES-FB parameters are lower compared to the stresses converted from the parameters obtained using the Fabric Kit method and the SEDDI Textura application. Furthermore, in the direct conversion of tensile and shear parameters obtained from the KES-FB system to CLO3D compatible units, a single elongation value determined at the maximum force is used, meaning the calculated stress parameter is based on just one value. In contrast, the Fabric Kit method, via the Emulator converter, utilizes five consecutive force readings at a defined elongation value, which, when examined in the F/ε diagram, represents a significantly broader testing range.

Digital prototypes, simulated based on SEDDI Textura mechanical properties, showed the closest match to real prototypes in both value and distribution of deformations, as shown in and . The advantage of AI-driven methods like SEDDI Textura is that they are deep learning models trained on large textile datasets, generalizing behavior beyond isolated measurements and capturing nonlinearities in structure/behavior relationships based on data patterns. These systems estimate parameter distributions rather than single values, increasing robustness to variability. Unlike standard physical testing methods, SEDDI Textura employs a multimodal approach that combines visual (2D fabric images) and structural inputs (weave type, fiber content, mass, and thickness), enhancing the precision of deformation predictions.

A pronounced symmetry of deformations was observed on the left and right sides of all digital 3D prototypes. In contrast, the real prototypes showed differences in the deformation’s distribution on the left and right sides. The observed limitation is a consequence of the computer 3D body model symmetry, as well as the symmetry of the kinematic transition of joints in the animation sequences.

The significance of the presented study lies in its integrative and comparative approach to evaluating the influence of different methods for determining fabric mechanical properties on the accuracy of 3D garment simulations under dynamic conditions. While numerous previous studies have investigated the fidelity of garment simulations using subjective visual assessments [,], cross-sectional comparisons [], or static 3D scanning methods [,], relatively few have focused on validating digital garment behavior through objective, quantitative analysis of deformation during motion. In contrast to studies that evaluate static drape accuracy or rely primarily on visual similarity [,,,], our research employs the ARAMIS optical 3D measurement system to capture and compare the dynamic deformations of physical and virtual garment prototypes. This methodological advancement enables a more precise and objective evaluation of simulation outcomes under realistic wearing conditions, addressing a major limitation identified in earlier research [,,].

By directly comparing three different methods for fabric parameter acquisition, KES-FB, Fabric Kit, and the AI-based SEDDI Textura application, within the same simulation environment (CLO3D), using identical garment models, textile material and human test subject, allows for a controlled analysis of how the source and quality of mechanical input data influence the resulting simulation fidelity. Notably, the findings demonstrate the potential of AI-assisted tools to generate accurate garment deformations during movement. Confirming the effectiveness of SEDDI Textura in predicting mechanical properties for 3D clothing simulation supports the advancement of sustainable, data-driven workflows in digital garment development [,,,].

## 4. Conclusions

The conducted research confirmed the feasibility of employing various methods for determining the mechanical properties of woven fabrics for digital 3D garment simulations under dynamic conditions. The integration of KES-FB, Fabric Kit, and AI-based SEDDI Textura into the CLO3D environment enabled realistic prediction of fabric deformation, which was validated through physical garment prototypes and 3D motion analysis. The ability to objectively evaluate physical prototypes in dynamic conditions, as demonstrated using the ARAMIS system, provides a reliable framework for assessing digital simulation outcomes and offers significant insights into the influence of mechanical parameters on 3D simulation accuracy, depending on the testing methods and protocols adopted by each measurement system.

The scientific contribution of this study lies in the quantitative comparison between simulated and actual garment behavior using an optical 3D measurement system for dynamic deformation, combined with advanced fabric characterization techniques. A comprehensive comparative analysis was performed between the deformation of digital and real garment prototypes under identical dynamic conditions, using the same garment models and materials. Methodologically, the study demonstrated the effectiveness of using the ARAMIS system for the quantitative verification of digital prototypes in the context of garment design, with allowance for ease, paving the way for its broader application in apparel engineering.

The study also highlights the potential of AI-based tools in replacing traditional testing setups with sustainable digital approaches. The validity of using AI technology (SEDDI Textura) to estimate mechanical parameters of textile materials, based solely on structural data and visual appearance, was experimentally confirmed, contributing to the advancement of sustainable digitalization methods without the need for conventional testing. The advantage of the SEDDI method stems from its combination of scalability, learning from large datasets, multimodal input, and optimization towards simulation outcomes rather than isolated measurements. Consequently, the simulation results generated using its predictions exhibit higher correspondence with the behavior of real garments, affirming its potential value for sustainable and industry-relevant apparel design.

The implications of the presented research findings can be observed from the practical, social and managerial aspects of application. This research confirms that the application of digital prototyping with the support of AI-based tools, such as SEDDI Texture, can significantly reduce the number of physical prototypes and the amount of textile waste, thereby reducing product development time and optimizing costs. The practical benefit for designers and manufacturers is an increase in the accuracy of material simulation, a reduction in material and transportation costs, and a faster response to changes in market demand. A particularly valuable contribution of this research is the introduction of a new methodology for the analysis and evaluation of prototypes using the ARAMIS optical 3D measurement system, which enables accurate measurement of fabric deformations and displacements. In this way, the results of digital simulation can be verified by real measurements, which ensures a credible interpretation of the results of digital analysis and increases the reliability of digital prototypes in industrial applications. The results indicate that the digital transformation of the textile and fashion industry has wider societal benefits through the reduction of waste, CO2 emissions and negative environmental impact. However, this transformation also opens up new challenges and opportunities in the field of employment and education.

New educational programs and curricula need to be developed that will enable young professionals and the existing workforce to acquire specialized digital skills, such as 3D modeling, working with CAD/CAM systems, digital prototyping, data management, and working with AI-based tools. This requires collaboration between industry, academia, and public policies in developing lifelong learning programs and adapting vocational education to the needs of Industry 4.0. In this way, the digital transition contributes not only to a more sustainable industry but also to strengthening employability, developing local communities and retaining talent. The findings indicate the need for managers in the textile sector to strategically plan investments in digital tools, staff training and adaptation of internal processes for the implementation of Industry 4.0. Organizations that adopt digital prototyping can gain a competitive advantage through faster innovation, resource optimization and more transparent supply chains.

Future research should be extended to include various fabric structures and garment types, with added focus on modeling textile finishing processes and refining AI-based predictive systems through deep learning algorithms and feedback from experimental results. The scientific insights gained from this study represent a meaningful step towards a more sustainable and efficient apparel development process and encourage further advancement of intelligent methods for virtual prototyping based on objective, digital, and automated approaches to material characterization.
